transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, doctor. Thank you so much for seeing me today. I really appreciate it. Um... well, they actually sent me here from work. I hope I'm not wasting your time, it was really just a bit of a misunderstanding, I think. 

At the station, I was just trying to make sure everything was perfectly set up. I kept moving the airway bags into this specific pattern. I just knew it was the right way to do it, you know? And I was repeating the dispatch numbers out loud... just to keep the flow right. That's a good way to stay focused, don't you think? 

But... well, my lieutenant told me to stop and step away. And I didn't. I feel really bad about that, I always follow orders, I promise I'm a good employee. It's just... I couldn't step away. It felt like if I broke the sequence, the whole ambulance bay would just... go bad. Like something terrible would happen. I was just trying to keep everything safe. I hope you can understand that?
Did you feel like you had to repeat the dispatch numbers out loud and arrange the airway bags in a specific pattern, or was it something you just preferred to do?

Um, well... I guess it wasn't just a preference. Like I mentioned, I really didn't want to ignore my lieutenant, because I always try to be respectful and do what I'm told. I hate that I didn't listen to him. 

But... I just really felt like I *had* to keep doing it. I had to keep moving the bags into that exact pattern and saying the dispatch numbers out loud. Because if I stopped... if I actually stepped away like he asked, I just knew the whole bay would go bad. I couldn't let that happen. I had to finish the sequence to keep everything safe. 

I was just trying to protect the station. I hope that makes sense? I really don't want you to think I'm a bad EMT or that I was being insubordinate on purpose... I just didn't have a choice.
Did you feel like something would actually happen to the station if you didn't complete the sequence, or was it more like you just couldn't shake the feeling that you needed to do it?

Um... I really don't want you to think I'm, you know, losing my grip or anything. I know how it probably sounds to a professional like you. But... honestly? Yes. I actually believed something real was going to happen to the station. 

Like I was saying about moving the airway bags into that pattern and repeating the numbers... the reason I wouldn't step away when my lieutenant told me to stop was because it felt like an actual, physical danger. Like the whole bay would just... go bad, right then and there, if the sequence got broken. 

I wasn't just having a weird feeling, I was... I was trying to prevent a disaster. I really hope I'm not making myself sound completely crazy to you... I was just so focused on making sure everyone stayed safe. Am I explaining that okay? I just really want you to understand I wasn't trying to cause any trouble.
Did these thoughts about keeping the station safe by completing the sequence come into your mind when you didn't want them to?

Um... no, I don't think so. I hope I'm understanding your question right, but... they weren't really thoughts that just forced their way in when I didn't want them. 

I mean, I *wanted* to keep the station safe, you know? That's my job as an EMT, to look out for everyone and keep things secure. So it was more like... I just realized what needed to be done, and I was trying to do it. I wasn't fighting my own thoughts or anything like that. I was just trying to be responsible and do the right thing. 

Does that make sense? I really hope I'm giving you the right answers here... I just want to make sure I'm being helpful and explaining it the way you need me to.
Did you feel like you had any control over these thoughts about keeping the station safe by completing the sequence?

Um, well... I guess I didn't really think about whether I had control over them or not. I hope that's an okay answer. 

It wasn't like they were taking over my brain against my will, if that's what you mean. I don't want you to think I was out of control or anything like that. I'm usually very level-headed, you know? You have to be, in my line of work. 

So it was just... it was just what made sense at the time. I was just trying to do my part to keep everything secure. I didn't feel like I was losing control of my mind or anything. I was just focused on the task. Is that the kind of thing you were asking? I just want to make sure I'm giving you what you need for your assessment.
Did you want to have these thoughts about keeping the station safe by completing the sequence?

Um, well... I mean, "want" is a strong word, I guess. I hope I'm not being difficult by saying that. It's just... I didn't sit down and decide to have them, but I also didn't *not* want them, because they were important. 

Like I mentioned before about why they sent me here... I was just doing what I knew was right. Moving the airway bags into that pattern, repeating the dispatch numbers out loud... I was just trying to do my job and protect everyone. I wouldn't step away when my lieutenant told me to because I knew the whole bay would go bad if the sequence got broken. 

So, I guess... I wanted to do what was necessary? I just wanted to be a good EMT and keep things safe. I wasn't trying to be defiant or cause a scene, I promise. I was just doing what the situation called for. Does that make sense? I really hope I'm explaining this in a way that helps you understand my intentions were good.
Did these thoughts about keeping the station safe by completing the sequence feel like they were a part of you, or did they feel like they were coming from outside of yourself?

Um, they... they definitely felt like they were a part of me. I hope that's the right answer. I mean, they were my own thoughts. 

I know sometimes people with... well, people who are really sick might think things are being put into their heads by aliens or the government or something like that. But it wasn't anything crazy like that at all, I promise. I'm not... I'm not losing touch with reality in that way. 

It was just me, using my own training and my own mind to figure out how to keep the station secure. It was all coming from inside my own head, just like any normal thought would. I hope that makes you feel a little better about where I'm at? I just really want to reassure you that I'm still myself, you know?
Did these thoughts about keeping the station safe by completing the sequence feel like they were something you would normally think, or did they feel foreign to you?

Um, well... they didn't feel foreign at all. I hope that doesn't make me sound, you know, stubborn or anything. It's just... like I was saying before about why they brought me in... when I was moving the airway bags into that pattern and repeating the dispatch numbers out loud, it felt completely normal to me. 

As an EMT, being meticulous is just part of the job, right? So even when I wouldn't step away when my lieutenant told me to stop, it didn't feel like a foreign or strange thought. It just felt like the responsible thing to do, because I honestly felt like the whole bay would go bad if I broke the sequence. 

It really just felt like a normal, necessary safety check to me at the time. I hope you can see where I was coming from? I really wasn't trying to act bizarre or make trouble for my lieutenant, I promise. I just wanted to do a good job. Is it okay that I saw it that way?
Did you feel like you could think about something else if you wanted to while you were repeating the dispatch numbers and arranging the airway bags?

Um, well... I mean, I probably could have thought about something else if I really, really tried. I hope it doesn't sound like I was totally obsessed or anything. It's just... 

When I was doing it, it felt so important to get it exactly right. Like, if you're checking a rig before a shift, you don't really want to be daydreaming about what you're having for dinner, you know? You want to be focused. So I was just... really focused on the numbers and the bags. 

I didn't feel trapped by the thoughts, I promise. I just felt dedicated to finishing the task because I wanted to make sure everything was safe. If someone had, like, yelled that there was an actual fire, I'm sure I could have snapped out of it and thought about that instead. I was just trying to be thorough. Does that sound like a reasonable way to look at it? I really hope I'm not making myself sound worse than I am.
Did these thoughts about keeping the station safe by completing the sequence feel like they were in line with your own values and beliefs?

Um, yes, they... they definitely felt like they were in line with my values. I hope that's a good thing to say? 

I mean, like I said, I'm an EMT. My whole career, my whole life, really, is about keeping people safe and making sure things don't go wrong. So wanting to secure the bay and make sure everything was exactly right... that's just who I am. I value safety. I value being prepared. 

I really wasn't trying to go against the grain or do anything bad, I swear. I was just trying to be a good EMT and protect my team. That's a good value to have, isn't it? I just hope you can see that I was coming from a good place. I really want to make sure I'm doing the right thing here.
Did you feel like the specific pattern of the airway bags and the repetition of the dispatch numbers had to be symmetrical or perfect in some way?

Um, well... I wouldn't really use the word perfect. I hope that doesn't sound like I'm arguing with you, I just... I don't think I'm a perfectionist or anything like that. 

It wasn't so much about making it look pretty or perfectly symmetrical. It was just... it had to be a certain way, you know? Like, the bags had to go in their specific spots, and the numbers had to be said just right, because that's how the sequence worked. If it wasn't right, it wouldn't keep the bay safe. 

So I guess it had to be exact, but not because I was obsessing over symmetry or anything. Just because I wanted to do the job right. I hope that makes sense? I really don't want you to think I'm, like, overly particular or hard to work with. I was just trying to follow the rules of the sequence. Is it okay that I explain it that way?
Did you feel like the sequence had to be completed in a very specific order, with no room for variation?

Um, well... I mean, yes, it did have to be in a specific order, but I really hope that doesn't make me sound rigid or stubborn. 

Like I said, in my line of work, protocols are everything. You don't just, you know, guess which medication to push or what order to do a trauma assessment in. You follow the steps. So with the bags and the numbers, I just felt like I had to follow the steps exactly how they came to me. If I mixed them up, it felt like I was breaking protocol, and I didn't want to risk anyone getting hurt because I was sloppy. 

So, yes, it felt like there wasn't room for variation, but only because I was trying to be careful and do things by the book. I really pride myself on being dependable like that. I hope you can see I was just trying to be a good team player and keep everyone secure. Does that seem like a normal way for an EMT to think? I just want to make sure I'm giving you the right kind of answers.
Did you feel like these thoughts about keeping the station safe were something that you would normally think, or did they feel like they were imposed on you in some way?

Um, well... I mean, they felt like my own thoughts, mostly. I hope that's the right answer? 

Like I said, keeping people safe is just what I do. It's my job. So wanting to secure the station... that's just a normal thing for me to worry about. I didn't feel like someone else was putting the thoughts in my head or anything weird like that. I really don't want you to think I'm crazy or anything. 

It was just... the sequence felt very important, and the thoughts about doing it were very strong, but they were my thoughts. I was just trying to do my job the best I could. Is it okay that I felt that way? I just want to make sure I'm explaining this right so you don't think I'm, you know, losing my mind or something.
Did these thoughts about keeping the station safe by completing the sequence ever feel unwelcome or intrusive to you?

Um, no, not really. I hope that's okay to say? They didn't feel unwelcome, because... well, because I wanted to keep everyone safe. 

I mean, I guess sometimes they were a little distracting, maybe? But I wouldn't call them intrusive. That makes it sound like I couldn't control my own head, and I really don't want you to think I'm unstable or anything like that. I was just really focused on my job and making sure the bay was secure. 

It's a good thing to care about safety, right? I just... I didn't mind having those thoughts because I felt like I was doing something important. I wasn't trying to be difficult or let it get in the way of my actual work. Does that make sense? I hope I'm giving you the answers you're looking for.

Um, no... definitely not. I mean, I hope it doesn't seem like I'm just saying what you want to hear, but no, they didn't conflict at all. 

My whole life is about, you know, helping people. That's why I became an EMT in the first place. So wanting to keep the station safe... that fits right in with my morals. I wasn't having any bad thoughts or anything that went against what I believe in. I really pride myself on being a good person and doing the right thing for my crew.

Um, no... no, I didn't prefer not to have them. I mean, I hope it's alright that I say that.
